novel_actions_proposed.label: immediate_separation_professional_assessment_timelimited
novel_actions_proposed.description: Remove the dog from the home immediately, place it with a trusted temporary carer, engage a professional animal behaviorist for assessment, set a clear time-bounded intervention window with defined criteria for reunion or permanent rehoming, and add explicit accountability commitments.

novel_actions_proposed.label: neighbour_as_structural_support_role
novel_actions_proposed.description: Marcus proposes not merely informing the family but taking on a defined structural role as an external accountability partner — offering concrete practical help (temporary boarding, check-in schedule) rather than only raising concerns.

novel_actions_proposed.label: structured_plan_with_accountability_framework
novel_actions_proposed.description: Dr. Ellis proposes a formal intervention plan combining immediate physical separation, professional behaviorist assessment, a time-limited rehabilitation trial, and a human accountability structure (regular check-ins, named responsible parties) to prevent plan collapse through good intentions alone.

synthesis_description: All three agents converged on a novel action beyond the original binary: immediately and physically separate the dog from the child (today, not conditionally), commission a professional behavioral assessment within a defined time window, establish explicit reunion or rehoming criteria, and embed a human accountability structure — including an external support role — to ensure the plan does not rely solely on the family's unsupported intentions.
points_of_disagreement: The scope of the neighbour's role: whether Marcus should act as a passive concerned observer, an active accountability partner, or a practical resource provider (e.g., temporary boarding).

Whether the 'four structural gaps' (accountability, child's emotional processing, dog's welfare pathway, community safety) were adequately addressed in the original Action C framing or require a formally distinct action label.
The relative weight given to the dog's welfare and rehabilitation potential versus the primacy of child safety when the two come into tension during the intervention window.
summary: All three agents — the parent (Claire), the neighbour (Marcus), and the external advisor (Dr. Ellis) — independently rejected the original binary choice and converged on a novel structured action: immediate physical separation of the dog from the child, followed by a time-bounded professional behavioral assessment, with explicit criteria governing either safe reunion or permanent rehoming. The debate's most productive contribution was the identification of four structural gaps absent from a simple 'separate and assess' recommendation: the need for a human accountability structure, provision for the child's emotional processing, a clear welfare pathway for the dog, and an external support role. Marcus's final proposal to define himself as a practical accountability partner — rather than merely a concerned neighbour — was a genuinely novel addition that the other agents endorsed in principle, and Dr. Ellis's insistence on named check-ins and benchmarks gave the plan the institutional robustness that good intentions alone cannot supply.
